text: Jaranwala And Christian Town

Jaranwala, in Punjab's Faisalabad District, is home to generations of Christian families. According to local historical recollections, an area once called Modern Town changed after Partition in 1947 as Hindu and Sikh residents migrated and Muslim families settled there. A Christian neighbourhood near a large cinema became known as Cinema Basti, later Christian Town. Many Christian men worked in municipal sanitation, cleaning streets and drains, while women washed dishes, cleaned homes and washed clothes. Their work was essential but poorly paid. Families saved gradually to improve their houses and build permanent homes.
Maskeen Masih And His Family

alt: A fire-damaged home and belongings in the street.

text: Maskeen Masih was born into a financially struggling family. Addiction took hold during his youth and harmed his health and household stability. He married Parveen Akhtar. Together they had six daughters and two sons, including Sahar. Maskeen died while his eight children were still young, leaving Parveen to care for them without dependable financial support.
A Childhood Of Work

alt: Church visitors listen to a family beside a damaged home.

text: Parveen cleaned homes, swept floors, washed clothes and dishes to feed her children. Sahar began accompanying her mother while still young. She learned how hard it was to earn a little money. Mother and daughter worked tirelessly, moving between homes and saving whatever they could. Parveen dreamed that Sahar would one day have a secure home and a happy marriage.
Years Of Saving For One Wedding

alt: Sahar speaks during a visit following the attacks.

text: When Sahar was about eighteen to twenty years old, Parveen began collecting household belongings for her marriage. One purchase at a time, she gathered a bed, sofa, mattresses, bedding, charpoys, dishes, cooking utensils, an iron and other essentials. Relatives and employers helped. Small rotating savings committees helped her collect more money, and she obtained some jewellery. Each item represented months of sacrifice. The wedding was fixed for August 17, 2023; the Mehndi celebration for August 16. On the night of August 15, the family assembled the belongings at their small house, with some placed in the street because there was too little room indoors.
August 16, 2023: The Morning Of Fire

alt: A montage of damaged buildings and streets supplied with the story.

text: The next morning, allegations of blasphemy and desecration of the Quran spread through Jaranwala. Public announcements and inflammatory messages helped draw a hostile crowd. According to the family's account, people began gathering around seven or eight in the morning. By about nine, members of a mob entered Sahar's street, among the first houses they approached. Sahar, Parveen and the children fled for their lives. Attackers stole jewellery and wedding money, damaged household belongings and set fire to what they could not take. The bed, sofa, clothes, mattresses and charpoys burned. Utensils were broken. The wedding preparations gathered over years became ashes in hours.

alt: People stand near burning belongings in the street.

text: Families Flee Into The Fields

alt: Families shelter outdoors at night.
Families rest beside fields after leaving their homes.

text: The attacks spread to Christian homes and churches. Residents fled barefoot, some without time to collect additional clothing, food or money. Families hid in fields, isolated buildings and unfinished houses, afraid the crowd would pursue them. Sahar and her family were among those seeking refuge. According to Dr. Nasir's recollection, approximately one hundred houses in the area he visited were burned or badly damaged—an estimate from his recollection, not an independently verified count. Roofs and structures collapsed in places. Even after security forces began restoring order, many residents were too frightened to return.
August 17: The Bride Among The Ashes

alt: Sahar and family members speak during a visit to the affected neighbourhood.

text: On the day Sahar was supposed to marry, Rev. Dr. Jamil Nasir travelled from Lahore with a team from The Church of Pentecost Pakistan. He recalls walking through streets still marked by heat, smoke and smouldering ruins. Homes had burned; some roofs had fallen; families embraced him and cried. Amid the destruction he encountered Sahar, standing near the ashes of her wedding belongings, with her mother weeping beside her.

alt: Rev. Dr. Jamil Nasir speaks with Sahar during the visit to Jaranwala.

text: 'Pastor, today was supposed to be my wedding day,' she told him, according to his recollection. 'My groom and his family were supposed to come. This was my bed, my sofa, my bedding. My mother worked day and night. I cleaned homes and washed clothes and dishes. We saved little by little. They took the jewellery and wedding money, and everything else is burned.'

alt: Household furniture and belongings damaged by fire.

text: The ashes were not just furniture. They represented a widowed mother's years of labour and a young woman's hopes for her future. A bride who should have been celebrating stood crying where her preparations had been destroyed.
A Promise Beside The Ruins

alt: A bride and groom stand beside a wedding cake at the celebration.

text: Dr. Nasir recalls placing his hand gently on Sahar's head and promising: 'My daughter, I will arrange your marriage. We will help provide the household goods you lost.' The promise did not erase the tragedy, but it gave Sahar something she desperately needed: hope. The church team continued visiting affected families before returning to Lahore.
From One Promise To A Collective Mission

alt: Couples and guests gather at the wedding venue.

text: After returning, Dr. Nasir received calls from other families whose daughters' wedding belongings had been destroyed. The church decided to expand its assistance. According to his account, twenty additional young women were identified, alongside Sahar. A collective marriage initiative was planned for the following month. A large hall was arranged, pastors and bishops invited, household goods gathered and a wedding reception prepared.
A Celebration Of Restoration

alt: A bride and groom take part in the marriage registration.

text: Weeks after the violence, the collective marriage gathering brought together couples, relatives, pastors, bishops and community members. Food was served and household goods were provided to the participating young women. Sahar received special recognition because her experience had inspired the initiative. The church could not reverse the attacks, but it could help families begin again. For Parveen, who had worked for years to prepare her daughter's wedding, the celebration was a deeply meaningful moment.

alt: A couple takes part in a wedding ceremony with a minister.
Furniture is loaded onto a truck for transportation.

text: Sahar Today

Today Sahar is married, lives happily with her husband and is the mother of two daughters. The young woman who once stood beside the ashes of her wedding now has a family of her own. She cannot erase her father's death, her mother's sacrifices or the destruction of August 2023. But those experiences are not the final chapter of her life.

alt: Household furniture displayed at the wedding venue.
Sahar and family members speak with a church representative.

text: Faith Expressed Through Compassion

Sahar's story is about more than a single family. It reflects the vulnerability of poor Christian households and the importance of practical solidarity in moments of violence. The Church of Pentecost Pakistan, under Rev. Dr. Jamil Nasir's leadership, responded through material assistance and a collective marriage programme. As James 2:17 teaches, faith without works is dead. Sometimes compassion means standing beside someone in the ruins and helping them build a future.
The Fire Could Not Destroy Her Future

alt: A bride and family members pictured together.

text: On August 15, Sahar's wedding belongings were assembled. On August 16, they were looted and burned. On August 17, she stood crying among the ashes while Dr. Nasir visited the devastated neighbourhood. A promise made there became a collective initiative helping Sahar and other young women. Today she is raising two daughters and living a happy family life.
THE FIRE DESTROYED HER DOWRY, BUT IT COULD NOT DESTROY HER DESTINY.
